summary: Mission Design is a free browser game for 1–4 players that teaches the trade-offs of space mission engineering. Players choose a goal, build a small spacecraft, and pick a rocket and an orbit while six limits pull against each other: mass, power, budget, data, communications and time. Then they fly a 30-day mission with random events (solar flare, ground-station outage, instrument glitch) and read a report that explains why the design succeeded or failed, so they can redesign and fly again. A round takes about 5 minutes and needs no installation. A bonus game, Rover Rules, teaches IF / ELSE IF / ELSE logic: players program a Mars rover with visual blocks and watch it drive over real terrain of Jezero crater (USGS data). The project answers the "Space Mission Design Game" challenge by letting students feel that every design choice is a compromise and that a failed mission is a lesson, not a game over. Orbit facts come from NASA Earth Observatory and NASA NSSDC pages; all other numbers are simplified for teaching and are not real spacecraft data.
details:
What it does. Mission Design is a browser game that lets students experience the core problem of space engineering: every choice costs something. The player picks a mission goal and difficulty, builds a spacecraft (instruments, solar panels, battery, radio, storage), chooses a rocket and an orbit, and watches a live dashboard of six limits: mass, power, budget, data, communications and time to launch. After launch a 30-day mission runs with seeded random events (solar flare, ground-station outage, instrument glitch, one solar wing opening only halfway, launch failure). A final report explains in plain words why the mission worked or failed, gives a 100-point score, and invites the player to redesign and fly again. The game supports 1-4 players, each with a role and a goal (teamwork score). A round takes about 5 minutes; no installation or account is needed.

Bonus game: Rover Rules. The player programs a Mars rover with visual IF / ELSE IF / ELSE blocks and watches it drive over a terrain grid built from real elevation data of Jezero crater (USGS Mars 2020 terrain-relative-navigation CTX DTM mosaic). The rover plans a route with A* path search, and the rules decide what it does when it meets slopes, sand or rocks.

Intended impact. Students aged about 10-18 learn that there is no perfect spacecraft, that margins matter, and that a failed mission is a source of learning. The page "Model notes" lists every formula (mass, power, battery in eclipse, data downlink, science value, rocket equation as background), what is simplified, and which numbers come from NASA pages, so teachers can use the game in class.

Tools and technology. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks and no build step; a seeded random generator so the same seed replays the same mission; Python (tools/prep_terrain.py) to convert USGS elevation data into a small terrain grid with computed slopes; GitHub Pages for hosting. Source code: https://github.com/kak0yt0-che1/rover

Creativity and design factors. We turned the engineering trade-off into a short, replayable loop (design - fly - read the report - redesign), added sound and a minimalist mission-control look, and kept honesty visible: game numbers are simplified, not real spacecraft data, and the project is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA. No NASA logos or mission identifiers are used.

Use of AI (Super Intelligence) tools. We used Claude (Anthropic) as an assistant: for brainstorming the game concept; for researching the challenge and the public NASA pages we cite; for writing, debugging and troubleshooting code (HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python), including the interface redesign made with Claude Code and the frontend-design skill; for writing and editing text and instructions in English; and for preparing this submission text. The voiceover of the demo video is AI-generated (synthetic voice); the video itself is a screen recording of our game with captions, and the video description and file metadata state that the voiceover is AI-generated. All AI-assisted code and text were reviewed and tested by our team. We did not use AI to generate NASA data; all NASA and USGS values come from the pages listed in the NASA Data and Other Data sections.
